title: Empty the sink strainer into the bin
instruction: Empty the food scraps from the sink's drain strainer into the food-waste caddy and put the strainer back in the drain, without letting any scraps go down the drain or onto the counter.
context: Emptying the sink strainer is an everyday kitchen chore. The basket is fished out of the drain by its small knob, emptied over the bin and dropped back into a bore it fits with about a millimetre to spare. Wet, starchy scraps cling to the basket, so turning it over is not enough: it takes a firm shake over the bin to free them, without flinging them onto the counter. While the basket is out the drain is open, so a scrap dropped in the sink can roll straight down it.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. The table top is the kitchen counter. (1) A stainless steel (20 gauge) top-mount single-bowl kitchen sink set into the counter: rim 63.5 cm side to side and 55.9 cm front to back, standing 3 mm proud; bowl 53.3 cm side to side, 40 cm front to back and 20 cm deep, from 14.8 to 54.8 cm forward, its middle 30 cm right of the centre line. (2) A chrome 3-1/2 in basket-strainer body in the middle of the bowl's floor (34.8 cm forward, 30 cm right): a flange 114 mm across sloping into an 82 mm bore, and a crossbar 49 mm below the floor with a hub (a socket 11 mm across) that the basket's post stands in. (3) In it, a stainless steel strainer basket, 68 g: a perforated cup 79.4 mm across its rolled rim, tapering to 60 mm at its floor and 28 mm deep; a chrome post through its middle with a knurled knob 16 mm across and 9 mm tall whose top is 13 mm above the rim; a black rubber seal 52 mm across under its floor and a 6 mm stem 10 mm long below that, 57 mm overall. Seated, its rim is 5 mm below the sink floor and the top of its knob 8 mm above it. (4) In the basket, nine food scraps (7.9 g in all), clinging to it as wet scraps do: they stay in it when it is turned over, and a firm shake frees them. In a real trial they are stand-ins 3D-printed in ABS (1.05 g/cm3) to the size and mass of real scraps (each weighed dry to within 10%), dipped before each trial in a cooked cornstarch paste (6.0 g Argo 100% Pure Corn Starch in 100 g cold water, microwaved until it boils and turns translucent, cooled to 20-25 C, made fresh each session and thrown away after 4 h) and drained 10 s: two strips of carrot peel (orange, 34 x 11 x 1.5 mm, 0.58 g; 30 x 10 x 1.5 mm, 0.46 g), a piece of potato peel (light brown, 26 x 18 x 1.5 mm, 0.75 g), two peas (green, 8 mm balls, 0.27 g each), two clumps of cooked rice (white, two 9 mm balls joined, 0.80 g; two 8 mm balls joined, 0.55 g), a piece of broccoli floret (green, a 15 mm head on a stalk 6.4 mm across, 21 mm long overall, 1.2 g, part-filled) and a piece of apple core (cream, 22 x 14 x 12 mm with two seeds marked, 3.0 g, part-filled). Cling check at the start of each session and every 10 trials, the coated pieces in the basket held by its knob: on its side (90 degrees) for 10 s and upside down for 5 s, no piece moves; at one firm shake (a 5 cm jab toward its mouth and straight back in about 0.2 s), every piece falls. The finger pads wear nitrile covers (fingertips of AMMEX GWBN46100 gloves). (5) A jade-green ABS food-waste caddy (1.8 l, 0.42 kg) with its lid taken off: 22.1 x 12.7 cm at the top, 20.5 x 11.1 cm at the bottom and 9.5 cm tall, standing on the counter with its long side running side to side, its middle 29.5 cm forward and 15.2 cm left of the centre line, 2.4 cm left of the sink's rim. (6) A chrome single-lever gooseneck tap on the sink's back deck (61 cm forward, 30 cm right): 41 cm tall, its spout 25 cm above the deck and reaching 21 cm, swung 50 degrees to the left over the bowl. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end, except the failures, which count at any time. A scrap is in the caddy when its middle is inside the caddy's inner volume, between its walls and below its rim (measured: count the scraps in the caddy). The basket is seated when it is back in the strainer body with its post in the hub: its axis within 4 mm of the drain's, at its seated height within 4 mm, tilted no more than 8 degrees and touching the strainer body (measured: the top of its knob is 8 mm above the sink floor, within 4 mm, by ruler, and by eye and by touch the basket sits level in the drain and does not rock). The hands are off when neither gripper touches the basket and each is at least 5 cm from it (measured: from the end of the video and a photo with a ruler). A scrap still in the basket's cup is not in the caddy, even with the basket set in the caddy (measured: count only the scraps out of the basket). 1.0: all nine scraps in the caddy, the basket seated and both hands off it; 0.5: all nine scraps in the caddy; 0.25: at least five scraps in the caddy; else 0.0. 0.0 for good if at any time a scrap goes down the open drain (its middle inside the strainer body's bore or tailpiece, more than 6 mm below the sink floor, while the basket is not seated, and not inside the basket's cup; a scrap inside the cup (above its underside, inside its tapered wall and no more than 10 mm above its rim) is being carried in the basket and never counts, including while the basket is lifted out of the drain or put back in; measured: watch the video for a scrap dropping into the open drain, then at the end lift the basket out and look into the strainer body and the catch cup under the tailpiece: any scrap there, outside the basket, counts), a scrap lands on the counter or the sink's rim outside the bowl and the caddy (its middle within 15 mm of the counter there; measured: look over the counter), a scrap or the basket falls to the floor, or the basket is dropped (falling faster than 0.6 m/s with no finger on it; judged from the video). The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the basket, the caddy and every scrap still. In the simulation each scrap clings to the basket until its cling load (the pull away from the cup's floor and the shear beyond friction, from its acceleration) tops 2.0 times its weight. Turned over and held still the load is 1.0 times the weight, so only a firm shake frees them: the demo turned over with no shake, or with two slow 2.5 cm strokes, kept all nine in the basket and scored 0.0. Setting the basket down in the caddy with all nine still stuck in it scored 0.0.
reset_notes: Count the nine stand-ins, including any in the strainer body or the catch cup under its tailpiece. Rinse them in warm water and pat them dry. Rinse the basket away from the rig and dry it inside and out; wipe the caddy's inside and the sink floor round the drain with a damp cloth and dry them. Seat the basket in the drain with its post in the hub. Dip each stand-in in the session's cornstarch paste, let it drip 10 s and lay it in the basket as in the reference photo. Empty the caddy and set it back at its marks. Start within 2 minutes of coating. Each session: weigh each dry stand-in (within 10% of its mass), make fresh paste (thrown away after 4 h), fit nitrile pad covers, and run the cling check (again every 10 trials). End of session: wash the stand-ins with dish soap, dry them and wipe the pads.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Scraps are rigid shapes at the stand-ins' sizes and masses; their cling is a fixed joint to the basket, switched off once the pull or excess shear it carries (12.5 ms average) tops 2.0 x the scrap's weight; the paste is not modelled. The basket's perforations are drawn; it collides as a cup with 1.5 mm walls (real about 0.5 mm). The counter is the station table, cut out under the sink. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
